items.title: The Korean War never formally ended
items.claim: How did the Korean War conclude?

options.text: An armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 by representatives of the UN Command, North Korea and China — but no peace treaty; the Koreas remain technically at war and the DMZ at the 38th parallel divides them

items.reveal:
Armistice negotiations began in July 1951 and lasted two years, largely over the issue of prisoner repatriation. South Korean President Syngman Rhee refused to sign and unilaterally released 27,000 North Korean POWs in June 1953.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) is 4 km wide and around 250 km long — one of the most heavily militarised borders in the world. Periodic incidents (the 1968 capture of USS Pueblo, the 2010 Yeonpyeong shelling) keep the conflict warm.

Moves toward a formal peace declaration have repeatedly stalled. The Korean War cost around 3 million lives — Korean civilians the majority — and shaped East Asian security for over 70 years.
items.why: Unresolved conflicts shape decades. The absence of a Korean peace treaty in 1953 is the structural foundation of every subsequent crisis on the peninsula.

items.title: Naseby (1645) was won by the New Model Army
items.claim: What was the Battle of Naseby?

options.text: On 14 June 1645, Parliament's New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax (with Oliver Cromwell commanding cavalry) decisively defeated Charles I's army in Northamptonshire — capturing his correspondence with foreign powers and ending hope of Royalist victory
A naval engagement in the English Channel
The first battle of the war (1642)

items.reveal:
The New Model Army had been formed by ordinance in February 1645 — the first national professional army, of around 22,000 men. Naseby was its first major test. Parliament's forces of around 14,000 defeated the king's 9,000.

The king's baggage train was captured, including his correspondence — letters showing he was negotiating with Irish Catholics and foreign Catholic powers for military aid. The 'King's Cabinet Opened' (published July 1645) destroyed remaining sympathy in Parliament.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in May 1646. He was handed to Parliament in 1647, tried for treason in January 1649, and executed on 30 January.
items.why: Single battles can decide wars. Naseby ended the Royalist field army; the king's captured letters ended any chance of negotiated settlement. The two together made the regicide of 1649 possible.

items.title: Newton published the Principia in 1687

options.text: 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, deriving Kepler's planetary laws mathematically — uniting terrestrial and celestial physics
A defence of the Aristotelian universe
A treatise on biblical chronology only

items.reveal_title: Standing on the shoulders of giants
items.reveal:
The Principia was published in Latin in July 1687, funded by Edmond Halley after the Royal Society's stock of unsold fish books left it short of cash. Newton derived the inverse-square law of gravity, the three laws of motion, and applied them to planets, comets, the tides and the shape of the Earth.

Newton had developed calculus (his 'fluxions') in 1665-66 during the plague closure of Cambridge. He published Opticks in 1704 in English.

Newton became Master of the Mint in 1699, prosecuting counterfeiters. He served as President of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727. His tomb is in Westminster Abbey.
items.why: Modern physics begins with one book. The unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics in 1687 is the high-water mark of the Scientific Revolution — and remained the framework of physics until Einstein.
